E0344.summary: A publication (new series, No. 13, 1845) that Atwood cites as the source of the English translations of an epitaph.
E0344.body: Atwood cites *The Critic*, new series, No. 13 (1845), as the source of the English translations of an epitaph she gives [I.1 ¶22] [I.1 n30]. It is a reference only.

E0345.summary: A cited source (Idem, p. 248) used to support the view that Intellect is a God-given sight which mortals lack through generation.
E0345.body: Atwood cites Crito (as “Idem, page 248”) in support of the view that Intellect is a sight given by God, which mortals lack through generation: “gave him a sight called Intellect, which is capable of beholding God” [II.1 ¶38] [II.1 n35]. She uses the passage approvingly.

E0346.summary: A disciple of Paracelsus whose *Philosophy Reformed* Atwood cites repeatedly and approvingly on the vital spirit in man, the true physician, and what the operator must be.
E0346.body:
Atwood names Crollius among the intelligent, worthy disciples of Paracelsus, with Van Helmont, Fludd, Helvetius and Faber [I.1 ¶64]. She notes that *The Philosophy of J. Crollius* carries the Addresses to the Athenians in English [I.1 ¶64]. She lists him as an adept, citing *Philosophy Reformed* in Pinnel's translation [I.1 ¶70] [I.1 n81].

She quotes him with approval on several points:
- **The vital spirit in man.** In *Philosophy Reformed* he holds that the gold-producing vapour is in man: “the same is the generating spirit of all creatures”. He also describes the true physician [II.1 ¶12] [II.1 n9] [II.1 ¶14] [II.1 n13].
- **Fire and the physician.** From *The True Physic*, chap. 1: “physic and pyrotechny, says Crollius, cannot be separated”. Atwood uses this for trial by fire, for the separation made by the natural inbred chemist, and for the physician born of the light of grace [III.1 ¶10] [III.1 n8].
- **Means of the work.** In the Admonitory Preface of Oswald Crollius, great things come from preparation, contemplation, handiwork and grace: “by a holy assiduity of preparations, joining thereto diligent contemplation of natural causes” [III.1 ¶13] [III.1 n12].
- **Who can do the work.** The slothful and profane are unfit: “these Chemical Secrets will never be fingered by those slothful or sottish despisers of them” [IV.1 ¶6] [IV.1 n4].

E0347.summary: The passage or condition under which the old life is crucified and a new one germinates: all is sown under it, and the soul must pass under it before regeneration.
E0347.body:
Quoting Jacob Boehme, Atwood gives the Cross as what one must enter “in the Fourth Form”, where Sol and Luna are together, in order to seek gold: “enter in even to the Cross, then seek gold and you will not be deceived” [III.1 ¶48]. Her own gloss speaks of crucifixion: “out of that crucifixion, by reunion of the principles under another law, the new life is elicited” [III.1 ¶49].

In her own voice, “All is sown under the cross and completed in its number” [III.3 ¶13]. Under the cross fire and water fall together and germinate. A reader's translation (ours, not the book's) has true Wisdom coming under it [III.3 ¶14]. She links this to “out of the crucifixion of the cerebral life” [III.3 ¶15].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the soul passes under its Cross before the residuum supplies its regenerate body, and the earth becomes its punctum saliens: “after that the soul has passed under its Cross” [APP ¶110].

The context suggests that the Cross stands for a death of the ordinary, cerebral life. A new life, joined under another law, then comes out of it.

E0348.summary: In Hermes as glossed by Atwood, the chief principle of the art: the Spirit of life in an obscured, passive state early in the work; one with the vulture.
E0348.body:
In a passage of Hermes that Atwood glosses, the Crow is the chief principle of the art. It is the Spirit of life in an obscured, passive state, at the early stage where the revived spirit is joined with its solar ferment: “the crow is also in the infancy of that work wherein the revivified spirit is united with its solar ferment” [I.3 n12].

It is identified with the vulture: “The vulture and the crow are interpreted to be one and the same thing, only differing somewhat in estate” [I.3 n12].

E0349.summary: Atwood's gloss on Hermes: the first visible resplendence of the vital tincture, the king triumphing over death when the colours appear.
E0349.body: Atwood explains the image directly: “By the crowned king, Hermes signifies the first manifested resplendence of the vital tincture” [I.3 n22]. The figure is the king triumphing over death when the colours appear. The meaning is stated by the text.

E0350.summary: The transparent state to which all things must be reduced before the Work truly begins.
E0350.body: Atwood writes that, before the Work truly begins, “all things are reduced to a crystalline diaphaneity” [IV.1 ¶48]. It apparently names a necessary preliminary state of complete clarity in the matter.

E0351.summary: The condition matter has lain under since the fall; the work aims to redeem matter from it.
E0351.body: For Atwood, the curse is the condition matter has lain under since the fall, and the aim of the work is to free matter from it: to “deliver matter from the original curse” and “to redeem matter from the curse, and to raise it from the dead” [IV.3 ¶38].

E0352.summary: A Church Father whom Atwood cites as taking up the rites of the Mysteries and veiling the church's mysteries in enigmas.
E0352.body: Atwood cites St Cyrillus as a Church Father who adopted the rites of the Mysteries. She uses him to support her claim that the church hid its mysteries in enigmas: “except in obscure terms, in such a manner, however, as that the faithful who are initiated may comprehend, and the rest be discouraged” [II.2 ¶3] [II.2 ¶5] [II.2 n9].

forms: D. Fabianus de Monte, S. Severin
E0353.summary: Author of *Tractatu de Emptione et Venditione* (Quest. 5), cited in a footnote for a definition of Alchemy.
E0353.body: Atwood cites *Tractatu de Emptione et Venditione*, Quest. 5, in a footnote. The words quoted are “Alchimia est ars perspicaci” [I.1 n52] (our rendering: Alchemy is an art for the perceptive). It is a reference only.

E0354.summary: A fable Atwood uses to illustrate the hand and fiery art bringing the metallic veins to light, as the hand expresses a thought formed beforehand.
E0354.body: Atwood uses the fable as an illustration: “Such were those Dactyli Idaei, literally the Fingers of Mount Ida” [IV.1 ¶34]. They stand for the hand and fiery art that bring the metallic veins to light, in the way the hand expresses a thought already formed.

E0355.summary: In a passage of Ricardus, something overthrown by the enigmas; the text does not define it.
E0355.body: In a sentence by Ricardus about study wiping away ignorance: “by these enigmas the Dagon is overthrown” [III.4 ¶20]. The text does not define it. The context suggests it stands for the ignorance that study removes.

E0356.summary: In Reuchlin as quoted: dark Aleph is the hidden essence, which becomes light Aleph when it shows itself to exist in human apprehension.
E0356.body: Atwood quotes Reuchlin. Dark Aleph is the hidden essence. It becomes light Aleph when it shows itself to exist in human apprehension: “is dark Aleph converted into light Aleph” [III.2 ¶10].

E0357.summary: In Boehme's scheme of the Three Worlds, a procreation or outer birth: a substance expressed from the internal and spiritual worlds.
E0357.body: In Boehme's Three Worlds, as Atwood gives them, the dark world is “a procreation or extern birth or, as it were, a substance expressed or spoken forth from the internal and spiritual worlds” [III.2 ¶16]. It is identified with the outer (“extern”) birth.

E0358.summary: In a passage of the Master, what the stone brings forth after Light: the clouds, called the mother of all things.
E0358.body: In a passage of the Master that Atwood quotes, the stone after the Light “brings forth the clouds, or darkness, which is the mother of all things” [III.1 ¶49]. Darkness is here equated with the clouds.

E0359.summary: An unattributed image Atwood uses as an analogy for the eclipse of the Divine Light in the hyperphysical work.
E0359.body: Atwood uses the image, without naming a source, as an analogy for the eclipse of the Divine Light during the hyperphysical work: “as there was darkness upon the Abyss when the Divine Spirit moved upon the Water’s face” [III.1 ¶60].

E0360.summary: Cited, via the 68th Psalm, on the Divine presence driving out what is alien, within Ripley's verse, and among the Hebrew prophets on the Wheel of Fire.
E0360.body: Atwood names David with Ezekiel, Moses, Zachariah and the Hebrew prophets in illustrating the Wheel of Fire, in which all things are transfigured [II.3 ¶54]. He is cited inside Ripley's verse about the waters passing away: “Abierunt in sicco flumina” [III.1 ¶57] (our rendering: the rivers went away into dry land). In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the 68th Psalm illustrates the alien being driven out when the Divine presence arises: “as wax before the fire” [APP ¶157].

forms: De Mainaduc, Puysegur, Colquhoun, Elliotson, Townshend, Dupotet
E0362.summary: A group Atwood praises as faithful pioneers of Mesmerism; she says the science has gone backward since them.
E0362.body: Atwood praises De Mainaduc, Puysegur, Colquhoun, Elliotson, Townshend and Dupotet as faithful pioneers of Mesmerism. She says the science has gone backward since their time [II.2 ¶6].

E0363.summary: A writer cited throughout the Appendix with approval, on numbers, the divine names, regeneration, and the earth as crucible of souls.
E0363.body:
All citations fall in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). Atwood praises him as having entered the centre of substantial life [APP ¶112–115]. She cites him approvingly on the following points:
- **The Crown.** With Behmen, he is the source of the phrase “the Crown” [APP ¶104].
- **Numbers.** From *Corresp.*, p. 298: “Numerical numbers are merely the bark of things” [APP ¶107]. Atwood extends this to outer nature and to scriptural tradition.
- **Correspondence**, letter 30, and *Theos. Correspondence*, p. 117. With Eckhartshausen, he is cited on the change in the circulation of the blood. He is also a reference on The Name speaking in us and on the mineral earth [APP ¶78] [APP ¶88] [APP ¶89].
- **The two Testaments.** From *Theos. Corresp.*, p. 244: their foundation lies “in the true pronunciation of the two great names” [APP ¶98]. Atwood glosses this as the revealed utterance of the life of God in man.
- **The regenerate body.** From *Tableau Naturel*, vol. 2, p. 230 (spelled “Se St Martin” there): “the earth is the crucible for souls as well as bodies” [APP ¶110]. He is cited on the residue of the sensual medium giving body to the regenerate soul.
- **Law and inquiry.** From *Reply*, p. 364, he is cited on a perfect law that works by degrees. His answers to a friend's particular question illustrate universal truth exploding questions, like the Hermetic inquiry [APP ¶112] [APP ¶113] [APP ¶115].

E0364.summary: In Norton, clay that has been heavily roasted; ground and mixed with good raw clay, it withstands fire.
E0364.body: Norton, quoted by Atwood: “Dead clay is called such a thing, As hath suffered great roasting” [III.4 ¶31]. Ground to powder and mixed with good raw clay, it withstands fire.

E0365.summary: In a quoted adept's verse, where the nucleus of Salt lies, to be guarded in holy silence; not explained.
E0365.body: A quoted adept, called “the mysterious adeptest”, speaks of Salt “whose nucleus in the Decad guard in holy silence” [III.3 ¶50]. The text does not explain the Decad.

E0366.summary: Diarist whose diary Atwood cites as evidence of Kelly's projection and of Kelly possibly revealing the secret to him.
E0366.body: Atwood cites Dee's Diary (n74: Sept. 1586) as a source for Kelly's projection and for the possible discovery of the secret: “Master E. Kelly did open the great secret to me, God be thanked.” [I.1 ¶66] [I.1 ¶67] [I.1 n74].

E0367.summary: The dead philosophers whose testimony, Atwood says, is the only evidence on which Alchemy can be imagined to be real.
E0367.body: Atwood says the testimony of defunct philosophers is the only evidence on which Alchemy may be imagined real [IV.4 ¶12].

E0368.summary: In Aristotle as reported by Atwood, the condition reached when the understanding touches its cause; only the duly initiated are capable of it.
E0368.body: In Atwood's report of Aristotle, deification is attained by contact of the understanding with its cause. Only the initiated can reach it: “duly initiated and capable of this deification” [II.1 ¶37].

E0369.summary: The creative fire the gods manifest through Intellect in Light, borne by Minerva as Phosphor; hidden from man by sensual conception.
E0369.body:
In Atwood's account, the gods manifest the Demiurgic Fire through Intellect in Light. “Minerva is sometimes called Phosphor, as being the bearer and measure of the Demiurgic Fire” [II.4 ¶26]. To Theurgists the gods show a self-visible Fire: “they exhibit to Theurgists a Fire which is itself, to itself, visible” [II.4 ¶29].

It is the creative fire borne by Wisdom. Ordinary sense-bound thinking hides it, “that Fire which the sensual conception occultates, and so forcibly restricts, that man does not suspect it even” [III.3 ¶71]. The context suggests it is the hidden fire the method seeks to release.

E0370.summary: That with which Theurgic sacrifice seeks to be joined; not further defined.
E0370.body: Atwood says Theurgic sacrifice seeks “a conjunction with the Demiurgic Intellect” [III.4 ¶25]. She does not define it further.

E0371.summary: A philosopher Atwood treats as an adept of the sacred art: his reduction of matter, the Fable of Proteus, and his pyrographic portrayal of the work.
E0371.body:
**Source and standing.** Atwood presents Democritus of Abdera, author of a book of Sacred Physics (*de Arte Sacra*), as treating the Hermetic art and the occult discovery under ancient philosophy. She names him as acquainted with the divine water [I.1 ¶12] [I.1 ¶20] [I.1 n14] [I.1 n20]. Synesius wrote a commentary on him [I.1 ¶27]. Norton's verse lists “Democrit” among masters who wrote obscurely: “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15]. Norton also reports him as naming the Water: “Lux umbra caresn, Water most orient;” [III.3 ¶74].

**The method.** Atwood endorses his proposal, as Bacon reports it, to reduce matter almost to annihilation and so free the spirit [I.2 ¶24]. Through the Fable of Proteus the matter, near annihilation, restores itself by an inbred force [I.3 n7]. The fable also supports binding the matter: “that method of working with nature is the most effectual that makes use of manacles and fetters” [I.3 n37]. He is cited for “Pan contains Proteus” [I.2 ¶36]. With Hermes, he repeats the process of the Vital Spirit [II.1 ¶25]. He hints that the changes stop only when Art brings the Matter into the fixity of its Final Cause [III.2 ¶22]. Following Bacon, Atwood calls the Experiment “the Art of Democritus” [III.3 ¶61].

**The Vulcanic action.** The *Flammelli Summula* gathers sayings from him. It shows, in operative language, the burning of the Brazen Body and Venus becoming golden: “Drawing the Fixed Brass out bodily” [I.3 n49] [I.3 n53]. Atwood says he portrays the Vulcanic action “before all, and as it were pyrographically”: “Drawing the fixed Brass out bodily, instructs this Abderite” [IV.1 ¶43] [IV.1 n40]. She calls him “our Abderite”.

Having seen it, he laughed at other things [IV.4 ¶27].

E0372.summary: Atwood's term for 'the whole' that is first not yet animated by its own returning light, later animated and shining from the dark abyss; apparently the whole subject of the work.
E0372.body: Atwood uses the name in two linked passages (spelled two ways). First: “For it is the whole Demogogon, as yet not actually animated by contact of his own returning light” [II.3 ¶30]. Later: “For it is the whole Demogorgon, now actually animated, which before was made visible without its subject light” [II.3 ¶52]. There it is ignited and shines from the dark abyss of being as a luciferous wheel. The text does not otherwise define it. The context suggests it names the whole subject of the work before and after its own light returns to it.

E0373.summary: Apparitional beings arising from the enclosed vapour of imagination, children of matter at war with the truth-seeking soul; also Hermes' revenging Demon that torments the wicked.
E0373.body:
**Atwood's account.** The demons of antiquity are apparitional beings born of a confined vapour of imagination: “all the race of demons, so much celebrated by antiquity, appear to have their origin in a life of this kind, viz., from an included vapor of the imagination” [II.3 ¶22]. They are called the children of matter: “as the progeny of matter, and as having an energetic virtue, but at natural war with the truth-seeking soul” [II.3 ¶24]. They are said to have sense, arts and an operative life, which they use to deceive, and they are given life by desire. The Chaldaic oracle also speaks of “pure demons”.

**Hermes (Poemander).** Among the wicked, the Mind gives way to the Demon: “giving place to the revenging Demon, which, applying unto him the sharpness of fire, tormenteth such a man sensibly” [III.3 ¶57]. When the body dissolves, this Demon receives the “idle manners”.

E0375.summary: That toward which even Matter extends, identified with the Good.
E0375.body: The text says even Matter is “extended to the desirable, i.e., to the Good” [III.4 ¶28]. It identifies the desirable with the Good. The speaker is unclear from the record.
